query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The degradation behavior of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 is primarily governed by the formation and evolution of surface oxide scales. Under oxidizing conditions, rapid and extensive oxidation of the reactive elements (Al and Ti) forms a thick, potentially porous mixed oxide that disrupts grain boundaries, while under reducing conditions the limited oxide formation preserves the integrity of the fcc matrix.
generation.material_initial_state: As-printed alloy with a fine, homogeneous fcc microstructure and minimal surface oxidation.
generation.intervention: Exposure of the alloy to elevated-temperature conditions (approximately 900°C) in controlled gas atmospheres—one oxidizing (e.g., air or an O2-rich environment) and one reducing (e.g., H2-containing) environment.
generation.conditions: Temperature maintained at around 900°C for durations ranging from 10 to 120 hours; gas compositions must be strictly controlled to represent clearly oxidizing versus reducing conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The nature (thickness, porosity, and adhesion) of the surface oxide scale, which modulates the integrity of grain boundaries in the fcc matrix.
generation.mechanism: In oxidizing atmospheres, reactive elements (Al and Ti) rapidly form a thick, mixed oxide scale that can be porous or poorly adherent, leading to grain boundary embrittlement and microstructural degradation. In contrast, in reducing atmospheres, the limited availability of oxygen results in a thinner and more protective oxide layer that helps preserve matrix cohesion and mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples exposed to oxidizing conditions are expected to show a significantly thicker, less adherent, and more porous oxide scale along with measurable decreases in hardness and tensile strength compared to those exposed to reducing conditions, which should exhibit minimal oxide buildup and better retention of the original mechanical integrity.
generation.baseline: Properties of the as-printed alloy at room temperature with an intact fcc matrix and negligible surface oxide formation.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold for temperature around 900°C under well-defined oxidizing or reducing gas compositions; variations outside these conditions (e.g., much lower or higher temperatures or mixed gas environments) may lead to different degradation behaviors.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative kinetics of oxide formation and precise correlations with mechanical degradation remain uncertain; additional studies are needed to determine the time-resolved evolution of the oxide scale and any potential contributions from minor phase transformations.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare several identical additively manufactured samples of Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 and expose them at 900°C in two controlled environments—one oxidizing and one reducing—for different durations (e.g., 10, 50, and 120 hours). After each exposure, characterize the surface using SEM, EDS, and XRD to determine oxide scale thickness, composition, and adherence. Concurrently, assess mechanical performance via hardness and tensile testing.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness, porosity, and composition (via SEM/EDS/XRD)
Grain boundary integrity and microstructural changes (microstructural analysis)
Mechanical properties (hardness and tensile strength) before and after exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxidizing and reducing conditions yield similar oxide scale characteristics and comparable degradation in mechanical properties, or if no clear correlation between oxide scale formation and mechanical degradation is observed, the hypothesis will be falsified.

Microstructure-Property Correlation and Its Evolution during Aging in an Al4.4Co26Cr19Fe18Ni27Ti5.6 High-Entropy Alloy

Abstract: AbstractThe efficient energy use in multiple sectors of modern industry is partly based on the efficient use of high-strength, high-performance alloys that retain remarkable mechanical properties at elevated and high temperatures. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) represent the most recent class of these materials with a high potential for high-temperature high-strength applications. Aside from their chemical composition and microstructure-property relationship, limited information on the effect of heat treatment as a decisive factor for alloy design is available in the literature. This work intends to contribute to this research topic by investigating the effect of heat treatment on the microstructure and mechanical performance of an Al4.4Co26Cr19Fe18Ni27Ti5.6 HEA. The solution annealed state is compared to aged states obtained at different heat treatment times at 750 °C. Study on the Corrosion Behavior of Additively Manufactured NiCoCrFeyMox High-Entropy Alloys in Chloride Environments

Abstract: This study aims to determine the optimal Mo content for corrosion resistance in two alloys, FeCoCrNiMox and Fe0.5CoCrNiMox. The alloys were fabricated using laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) technology with varying Mo contents (x = 0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.15). The corrosion behavior of these alloys was investigated in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution at room temperature and 60 °C using electrochemical testing and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). The results show that all alloys exhibit good corrosion resistance at room temperature. However, at 60 °C, both alloys without Mo addition exhibit severe corrosion, while the Fe0.5CoCrNiMo0.1 alloy demonstrates the best corrosion resistance while maintaining the highest strength. The enhanced corrosion resistance is attributed to the optimal molybdenum addition, which refines the passive film structure and promotes the formation of Cr2O3. Furthermore, molybdenum oxide exists as MoO42− ions on the surface of the passive film, significantly improving the alloy’s corrosion resistance in chloride-containing environments.

Selective electron beam melting of Al0.5CrMoNbTa0.5 high entropy alloys using elemental powder blend

Abstract: AbstractHigh Entropy Alloys (HEAs) is a novel promising class of multi-component materials which may demonstrate superior mechanical properties useful for high-temperature applications. Despite the high potential of HEAs, their production is complicated, using pre-alloyed powders in powder metallurgy route. This significantly complicates development and implementation of refractory BCC solid solution based HEAs. The present paper reports on experiments aiming at production of Al0.5CrMoNbTa0.5 multi-principle alloy using powder bed beam based additive manufacturing. Samples were manufactured using Selective Electron Beam Melting (SEBM) additive manufacturing technique from a blend of elemental powders aiming at achieving microstructure with high configurational entropy. Though it was not possible to achieve completely homogeneous microstructure, the as-printed material was composed of the zones with two multi-component solid solutions, which differed only by Al content confirming in situ alloying.
